events.title: TWENTY LOCAL VETERANS ARRIVE AT VALERIUS'S COLUMN
events.body: Twenty Roman veterans make themselves known to Valerius after hearing of his growing influence and the reputation that has followed the expedition through the surrounding territories. They present themselves as men who have served long enough in the region to know its roads, water sources, settlements, seasonal difficulties, and the habits of communities beyond the immediate Roman camps. They ask for no enlistment payment and instead request only that, if accepted, they eventually serve in Valerius's personal guard, where they believe their accumulated experience would be most useful. Valerius refuses to grant that position merely on reputation and tells them that their claim must be demonstrated in the field. The twenty agree to prove their worth before their admission is made permanent.

events.title: THE VETERANS BEGIN THEIR PROVING MARCH
events.body: The twenty veterans are given no special privileges during the first stage of their trial. Valerius sends them ahead under observation with the task of identifying practical routes between the expedition's present position and the known sections of the engineered road without relying on the expedition's existing route register. Their value is tested against what they actually know rather than what they claim to know. They identify several usable approaches, distinguish ground that becomes difficult after rain, and point out places where a traveler would naturally seek water. Their information is checked against the expedition's existing observations before any decision is made about their admission.

events.title: TITUS VARENUS CORRECTS THE COLUMN'S ROUTE ASSUMPTION
events.body: During the second stage of the proving exercise, Titus Varenus identifies a route that appears shorter on the expedition's working map but becomes impractical farther ahead. He explains the local ground in terms of an old seasonal drainage path and directs the scouts toward a higher approach that remains passable. The expedition's scribes compare his account with the terrain immediately at hand and find that his warning corresponds with the physical ground. Valerius treats the demonstration as evidence of useful local knowledge rather than as proof that Varenus should command the others. The other veterans remain under the same proving conditions and continue working as a group.

events.title: THE TWENTY VETERANS TEST THEMSELVES AGAINST THE LOOSE PHALANX
events.body: Valerius brings the veterans into the expedition's established loose-phalanx drill so that their local experience is tested alongside their ability to function within his existing doctrine. The veterans initially tighten their spacing more than the formation requires, but after instruction they adopt the deliberate intervals and outward-facing watch used by the rest of the column. Their experience proves useful in identifying where the formation can safely pause without losing access to water or obscuring the surrounding approaches. By the end of the exercise, the twenty are no longer being judged simply as men with stories about the territory; they have demonstrated that their knowledge can be integrated into the expedition's actual field method.

events.title: THE VETERANS FIND A SECONDARY WATER SOURCE OMITTED FROM THE EXPEDITION REGISTER
events.body: A small detachment of the veterans identifies a secondary water source near an established approach that does not appear in the expedition's existing register. The discovery does not prove that the source is permanent, and the veterans themselves caution that its usefulness depends upon the season. Their warning prevents the expedition from treating the find as a guaranteed supply point. The scribes record both the location as a local reference and the limitation attached to it, preserving the distinction between veteran knowledge and a fully surveyed logistical asset. Valerius orders the source investigated further before it is incorporated into future movement planning.

events.title: THE TWENTY COMPLETE THE FINAL TERRAIN TEST AND EARN ADMISSION
events.body: The veterans complete the final stage of their proving exercise by guiding the column through a sequence of familiar and unfamiliar approaches while maintaining the same discipline expected of every other member of the expedition. Their reports remain consistent with what the expedition can independently observe, and they demonstrate that they can distinguish remembered local knowledge from assumptions about places they have not personally examined. Valerius accepts the result and admits all twenty into the expedition as permanent men. Their requested personal-guard role is also accepted as the condition under which they volunteered, but their place in that guard is now grounded in demonstrated service rather than reputation alone.

events.title: THE NEW GUARD VETERANS BEGIN WORKING THE OUTER WATCH
events.body: The twenty veterans begin their new duty without displacing the expedition's established officers or rewriting the existing formation doctrine. Titus Varenus and the other veterans are distributed through the outer watch so that their knowledge of local approaches can complement rather than replace the expedition's existing scouts and scribes. Valerius keeps the group under the same discipline as the rest of the column and requires their local reports to be recorded when they materially affect a route, water source, settlement, or other geographic observation. The arrangement gives the expedition a permanent local-experience component while preserving the distinction between direct observation and remembered knowledge. The personal guard therefore begins as a working field institution rather than an honorary title.
